sections.title: Other project ideas
paragraphs: The following pros and cons are retrospective assessments added to this report. They are not confirmed statements from the meeting or reasons for individual votes.

tables.label: Project idea comparison
rows: Docent: multilingual exhibition guide
A clear setting for follow-up questions and multilingual conversation.
Official exhibition materials can ground answers.
A pilot can start with one exhibit and one tablet.
Realistic testing needs an exhibition partner.
Noise and reluctance to speak in public may limit use.
Content updates and answer checks require ongoing work.
VoiceQuest: multiplayer voice mystery game
Team members can test the game together.
The game tests turn-taking, interruptions, and shared context.
One short mystery gives the prototype a clear scope.
Enjoyment depends heavily on story quality.
Simultaneous speakers make interaction difficult.
Spoilers or inconsistent clues can break the game.
VoiceFit: voice-controlled workout assistant
Hands-free control addresses a concrete inconvenience.
Timers, pauses, and corrections give measurable tasks.
User-defined routines reduce the need for specialist content.
Existing timers may already meet user needs.
Breathing and background noise can reduce recognition quality.
Incorrect timing or commands can disrupt exercise.
Reservation assistant: AI phone bookings
The service completes a concrete task.
It can reach businesses without online booking.
It tests conversation, negotiation, and delegated actions.
Phone integration adds cost and complexity.
Staff may decline or struggle with AI calls.
Ambiguous answers can cause incorrect booking confirmations.
Voice body double: help with task completion
The service addresses difficulty starting and finishing tasks.
It tests proactive check-ins and persistent task state.
Completion and repeat use give concrete evaluation measures.
Check-ins may feel intrusive or like nagging.
Scheduling and reconnection add complexity.
Use may decline after the initial novelty fades.
FamilySync: shared family scheduling
The service addresses recurring coordination needs.
It tests multi-user context and consent.
A three-person scenario gives a focused prototype.
Adoption needs participation from several family members.
Speaker identification and calendar access add complexity.
Permission or schedule errors can undermine trust.

sections.title: Overtime discussion: everyday reflection
paragraphs: After the meetup, a few members explored a lighter role than specialized mental healthcare. These ideas did not finalize the product scope.

after.title: Service role: everyday reflection
paragraphs: The team explored help with expressing and organizing everyday thoughts, with a lighter role than specialized mental healthcare.

after.title: Speak, organize, gain distance, notice patterns
items: A hands-free brain dump could let users speak freely instead of typing, then review an organized account of their day.
Distance from their thoughts may help users view situations more objectively and notice recurring triggers or patterns. A personal checklist was suggested.

after.title: Conditions for use and trust
items: Users need private time and a space where they can speak comfortably. Some users value writing by hand, so the team must examine when speech is useful.
People may share worries with a trusted listener who helps them notice assumptions, biases, mistaken judgments, or leaps in reasoning. A diary or spoken account can still be selective or incomplete.

records.title: Third regular meetup: voice tarot and team development
records.venue: Hyundai Motor and Kia headquarters, Yangjae
records.summary: The team changed the MIND DETOXING concept to voice tarot. The first version will use a mobile website with an immediate voice connection. The product name and voice provider remain open.

sections.title: Decisions from the meeting
items: Build a two-way tarot conversation. The user explains a question, selects a card, hears an interpretation, and asks follow-up questions.
Start with a mobile website. The user starts a voice session inside the website. A telephone number is not necessary.
Use a cute, playful visual direction. The team still needs to choose the character and detailed design.
Consider scheduled calls and payments after the immediate connection works.
Let members work on features across disciplines. Product, frontend, and backend coordinators will help resolve differences.
The goal is a working product and a successful December 16 demo. Sona remains an optional tool.

sections.title: What the discussion clarified
items: The same product description led to different expectations. The specification must show the screens and conversation sequence together.
The reader must speak the interpretation. A spoken greeting followed by a text-only result does not meet the intended experience.
Do tests of Korean pronunciation, response delay, interruption, and character tone with real conversations.
Compare OpenAI and ElevenLabs before the provider decision. Their APIs have different interfaces.

sections.title: Progress and remaining work
items: The team selected the product direction. A working product and live voice test results are not yet available.
The next checkpoint is one complete mobile flow: start, conversation, card selection, spoken interpretation, and end.
The proposed schedule has a November 30 demo milestone. Presentation practice follows. The submission dates need confirmation from the organizer.
The leader will prepare the first specification, API comparison, and shared development setup. Members will review the specification and select tasks.
Make a decision about the intended users, name, character, provider, cost limits, hosting, and task owners.

sections.title: GitHub and Codex workflow proposal
items: These are proposed rules for development after v1.0. The meeting did not approve these detailed procedures.
Create an Issue before each task. Record the purpose, scope, acceptance criteria, owner, and reviewer.
Create one branch per task from the latest main branch. Do not commit directly to main.
Ask Codex to read AGENTS.md and the Issue. Examine its plan before implementation.
Open a small draft pull request early. Include the Issue, reason for the change, test results, and screenshots when applicable.
Ask another member to examine the change and user flow. Use Codex code review as additional help.
The leader is the first integration maintainer. This person examines the peer review and CI results before a squash merge.
Another member must examine the leader’s changes. Select a second integration maintainer for absences.
Resolve conflicts with the other task owner. Ask the relevant coordinator for help with product or interface decisions.
Use CI for type checks, lint checks, tests, and the build. Use test adapters without production secrets or paid API calls.
Deploy main to a test environment after checks pass. Check the main user flow before deployment to the demo environment.
Use GitHub Projects: Backlog, Ready, In progress, In review, and Done. Mark work Done after deployment verification.
Keep keys, raw audio, and personal conversations out of the repository. Record contributions through results, reviews, tests, and documentation.
Ask each member about preferred work, available time, blockers, and support needs. Record important decisions in the repository.
